disclaimer: Interactive FireOpsSim study decks are preparation/reference only. They are not official skill sheets, provider cards, or FEMA certificates. Verify department SOPs, state/AHJ rules, medical direction, adopted codes, manufacturer procedures, and current issuer/FEMA course editions.

firefighter_1.label: Firefighter I
firefighter_1.summary: Core structural-firefighting knowledge: PPE/SCBA, fire behavior, hose, ladders, search, and safety. Preparation only—follow your academy and certifying authority.
guide: PPE and SCBA
Inspect, don, and check interfaces before entry. Treat low-air as a cue to follow department air-management policy, not a target for remaining inside.
Fire behavior
Heat transfer, ventilation-limited fire, flow paths, and door control change interior conditions as soon as an opening is made.
Hose and nozzles
Deploy, flake, charge, and advance with nozzle and backup communication. Fix kinks before blaming water supply.
Ladders and search
Select a ladder for the objective, maintain crew integrity, and keep an exit plan during oriented search.
Mayday readiness
Know how to declare emergency traffic, stay oriented, and support RIC without becoming a second victim.
cards: The route heated gases, smoke, and air move between higher- and lower-pressure areas or openings.
Hood, gloves, coat, and facepiece gaps are common failure points during heat and work.
Act on department air-management policy; it is not a remaining-work target.
An opening can add oxygen and strengthen a flow path before suppression is ready.
A systematic pattern, partner contact, communication, and a planned exit.
What belongs in a skill log?
De-identified skill, repetitions, feedback, and lessons—not PHI or official sign-off.
quiz: Before forcing a smoke-charged exterior door, you should:
Coordinate the opening with the line/search plan and read conditions
Openings change ventilation and fire behavior.
The best reason to study building construction is to:
Recognize fire-spread and structural risk clues
Construction knowledge supports risk recognition, not fortune-telling.
A charged attack line will not advance because of kinks. First action:
Clear hose management and communicate with the operator
Hose management often solves apparent pressure problems.
Orientation, emergency traffic, and crew integrity
Leaving your partner to find a window
Rare high-consequence skills degrade without rehearsal.

Ask an instructor what 'good' looks like on your department's skill sheets.

firefighter_2.label: Firefighter II
firefighter_2.summary: Company-level coordination: ventilation timing, search, salvage/overhaul, standpipe concepts, and supporting command. Confirm JPRs with your certifying agency.
guide: Coordinated ventilation
Vent timing, location, and method must match suppression and search—not happen as a standalone task.
Search with conditions
Primary search priorities change with fire location, staffing, and ventilation. Keep crew integrity.
Standpipe / high-rise support
Pack arrangement, floor control, pressure considerations, and communications matter more than a single formula.
Salvage and overhaul
Protect property and evidence while finishing the fire problem. Watch for hidden fire and structural compromise.
Company communications
Concise progress, needs, and hazards keep the officer's picture current.
cards: Openings can change fire behavior, interior tenability, and search conditions.
Firefighter rescue support—not a secondary attack crew unless reassigned.
Location, task, conditions, needs, and anything that changed the plan.
Hidden fire, structural compromise, and evidence preservation can all be in play.
Get a working line to the fire floor with the right fittings, length, and communication.
When risk/benefit, conditions, resources, or progress no longer support it.
quiz: Ventilation before water on fire is risky because:
It can intensify the fire and worsen interior conditions
A strong Firefighter II habit is:
Skipping salvage until the next shift
If conditions change during search, you should:
Communicate the change and reassess with your officer
Changing conditions require a new picture.
Balance fire extinguishment, property protection, and documentation
Do not destroy evidence unnecessarily, but finish the fire problem.
next: Run a coordinated ventilation tabletop.
Practice a standpipe pack layout on the floor.
Use Fireground Decision Sim after studying the topic.

hazmat_awareness.label: HazMat Awareness
hazmat_awareness.summary: Recognize, isolate, deny entry, and notify. Awareness does not authorize offensive product control.
guide: Stay in scope
Awareness actions are recognition, isolation, notification, and protective-action support—not rescue in the hot zone.
Scene clues
Occupancy, containers, placards, labels, shipping papers, and witnesses all matter. Do not guess a product.
Isolation
Use current ERG/protective-action guidance and local SOP for initial isolation and downwind concerns.
Notifications
Who needs to know, what they need, and which specialty resources come next.
ERG use
Treat the ERG as an initial decision aid, not a complete product SDS or incident action plan.
cards: Offensive product control or hot-zone rescue unless trained and assigned otherwise.
Scene clues plus current references—not a guessed chemical name.
To protect responders and the public while more information is gathered.
Vapors and smoke can travel and expose people who are not at the source.
Product clues, isolation in place, wind, exposures, and what you still do not know.
Treat as a worst reasonable case until identified.
quiz: You see a placard but cannot read the ID number. You should:
Isolate, deny entry, and use current references while gathering more clues
Walk up to the tank for a better look
Do not close the distance to unknown product.
Begin diking in the hot zone
Recognize, isolate, notify, and support protective actions
The ERG is best used as:
An initial isolation and protective-action aid
Follow current ERG and local protocol together.
next: Practice placard recognition.
Walk an isolation tabletop with a map.
Confirm your department's Awareness SOG.

hazmat_operations.label: HazMat Operations
hazmat_operations.summary: Defensive operations: zones, decon support, PPE limits, and resource requests within Operations scope.
guide: Zones
Hot, warm, and cold zones control access. Adjust for wind, terrain, and changing product information.
Defensive actions
Isolation, diking concepts, vapor suppression concepts, and waiting for specialty resources based on risk.
Decon support
Corridor flow, contamination control, and protecting the cold zone. Follow local decon SOP.
PPE limits
Protective clothing has limits. Do not invent product certainty to justify the wrong ensemble.
ICS support
Clear objectives, accountability, and resource requests keep Operations work inside command.
cards: Operations can support defensive control and decon; Awareness primarily recognizes and isolates.
Support, decon, and controlled access—not a second hot zone.
To prevent spreading contamination to uncontaminated people and equipment.
Entering to plug a leak without training, PPE, and assignment.
What you have, what you need, product clues, and exposures.
When risk, PPE limits, or unknown product exceed your level and assignment.
quiz: Have a clear dirty-to-clean flow and contamination control
Be set up inside the hot zone
Choosing PPE at Operations level should:
Use current references and department policy
PPE has limits; policy and references matter.
A defensive option when trained, equipped, and assigned
If the product remains unknown, you should:
Keep isolation and treat as a worst reasonable case
next: Set up a decon corridor walk-through.
Run an isolation tabletop.
Review current ERG protective-action pages.

hazmat_technician.label: HazMat Technician
hazmat_technician.summary: Technician work is agency-specific. Use this deck for planning and support concepts—not as a substitute for technician training, SOPs, or medical direction.
guide: Training boundary
Technician offensive control, monitoring, and specialized PPE require current training, medical clearance, and assignment.
Information quality
SDS, shipping papers, monitoring, and technical specialists beat guessing.
Control options
Containment, confinement, and recovery decisions depend on product, container, and risk—not a single favorite tactic.
Support the team
Research, logistics, decon, and medical monitoring often determine whether an entry is even possible.
Documentation
Actions, readings, times, and exposures matter for safety and later investigation.
cards: Current training, medical clearance, PPE, and an assignment inside ICS.
To match PPE, tactics, and medical support to the actual hazard.
Inform decisions—not to create a false sense of safety by itself.
Work one variable at a time and communicate readings and limits.
The incident's command/safety system, not individual initiative.
Decon, medical monitoring, documentation, and a debrief of what changed.
quiz: Trained, equipped, assigned, and the risk/benefit supports it
Be ignored if you have a placard
If readings exceed your ensemble limits:
Documentation after a technician operation should include:
Actions, times, readings, exposures, and remaining hazards
Records support safety and later review.
next: Review your agency technician SOGs.
Practice research and ICS support roles.
Do not use this deck as a technician skill sheet.

driver_operator_pumper.label: Driver / Operator — Pumper
driver_operator_pumper.summary: Safe driving, placement, pump systems, hydraulics, water supply, and troubleshooting. Use department hose/nozzle packages—not generic coefficients alone.
guide: Arrive and place
The first job is getting the apparatus and crew there safely and positioning for hose, water, and later units.
Pump systems
Know intake/discharge paths, gauges, governor/relief, primer, and abnormal indications for YOUR apparatus.
Hydraulics
PDP accounts for nozzle pressure, friction loss, elevation, and appliances. Mental math is a reasonableness check.
Water supply
Hydrants, residual, drafting, relay, and tenders. Watch residual as demand changes.
Troubleshoot one variable
Supply, valves, air leaks, cavitation, then discharge-side causes. Do not change everything at once.
cards: Safe driving and placement for operations.
The pump is not receiving enough water for the demand.
Its change while flowing helps judge how supply responds to demand.
Real targets depend on department equipment and SOP.
Source, intermediate, and attack pumpers with communications and pressure discipline.
Opening or closing valves too quickly can damage hose, fittings, and the system.
quiz: Residual drops sharply as more lines open. You should:
Communicate and reassess demand versus supply
A large residual change is a water-supply clue.
Correct pump math but poor placement equals:
Only one part of operator performance
Driving, placement, systems, and communication all count.
If the pump will not prime from draft:
Check gaskets, caps, strainer, lift, and air leaks
Air leaks and setup beat more primer time.
Change one variable and watch the result
Cause and effect disappear if you change everything.
next: Build a department-specific pump card.
Run a hydrant residual drill.
Practice failure recognition monthly.

driver_operator_aerial.label: Driver / Operator — Aerial
driver_operator_aerial.summary: Placement, stabilization, load awareness, and aerial-device operation. Follow manufacturer procedure and department SOP—never this deck alone.
guide: Spotting
Place for the objective, collapse zones, overhead hazards, later units, and outrigger/stabilizer room.
Stabilization
Set the device per manufacturer and department procedure before raising. Confirm indicators.
Load and reach
Know rated capacities, tip loads, and how extension/angle/personnel change the picture.
Communications
Operator, officer, and team at the tip need closed-loop communication.
Driving
Length, height, weight, and swing matter in traffic and on the fireground.
cards: To find overhead wires, grade, surface, and space for stabilizers.
Angle, extension, waterway, and personnel/equipment at the tip.
Do not spot or operate in the area a wall or aerial could occupy if it fails.
Only if manufacturer and department allow it for that surface and objective.
Stop, make it safe, and follow the apparatus procedure—do not override casually.
quiz: Before raising the aerial you should:
Ignore grade if you are in a hurry
Overhead wires near the objective mean:
Re-spot or choose another access method
Use the stick as a probe
Electrical and overhead hazards control placement.
A manufacturer limit that changes with configuration
Know the chart for the setup you are in.
Short, closed-loop, and tied to the objective
The operator needs a live picture.
next: Review your apparatus operator manual with an instructor.
Practice spotting on the apron.
Use Fireground Decision Sim for placement context.

fire_officer_1.label: Fire Officer I
fire_officer_1.summary: Company-level leadership: size-up, assignments, accountability, coaching, and risk. You own crew safety and communication, not only task completion.
guide: Size-up
Building/occupancy, conditions, life hazard, access, resources, water, and initial actions—concise and useful.
Assignments
Every assignment needs a task, location, objective, and communication path.
Accountability
Know where crews are, what they are doing, and when conditions require a PAR.
Coaching
Set the standard, observe, give specific feedback, and get another repetition.
Risk
Strategy should change when risk/benefit, conditions, or resources no longer support it.
cards: You own crew safety, coordination, development, and decision consequences.
Unit ID, building/occupancy, conditions, actions, needs, and command.
Clear task, location, objective, and how to talk back.
When conditions, risk, resources, or progress no longer support it.
Specific observation, the standard, and another corrected repetition.
Training, education, relevant experience, and continuing education.
quiz: A crew finishes an assignment as conditions change. You should:
Reassess, communicate, and align the next action with strategy
The first radio report should be:
Concise, actionable, and complete enough to set command up
Delayed until the fire is out
Length is not the goal—usefulness is.
You cannot say where people are or what they are doing
Location and function must be known.
A promotional plan built only on certificates is incomplete because:
Education, experience, and continuing education also matter
Development is more than a wall of certs.
next: Deliver three size-ups out loud this week.
Lead a short company drill.
Run Fireground Decision Sim from the officer seat.

fire_officer_2.label: Fire Officer II
fire_officer_2.summary: Beyond the first-arriving company: multi-company coordination, performance management, documentation quality, and improvement work.
guide: Multi-company operations
Sectors/groups, span of control, and clear objectives for more than one crew.
Performance
Expectations, evaluation, coaching, and documentation that would stand review.
Projects
Process improvement, training plans, and evidence of leadership beyond a single incident.
Communication
Up, down, and across—written and verbal. Ambiguity creates safety and personnel problems.
After-action
Capture what worked, what failed, and the next repetition for the company and the department.
cards: Too many direct reports reduces supervision quality.
Facts, one strength, one gap, and a next drill—not blame theater.
Timely, factual, and complete enough for the next supervisor or investigator.
FO II leans more into systems, multiple companies, and organizational communication.
A problem, a measure, a trial, and a follow-up—not only a meeting.
Give a complete picture: strategy, assignments, resources, and hazards.
quiz: Two companies are working overlapping objectives. You should:
Add a third company to the same task
Overlap without coordination wastes people and creates risk.
Personnel documentation is strongest when it is:
Factual, timely, and tied to expectations
The record has to be usable later.
A process-improvement project should start with:
A clearly defined problem and a way to see change
Nothing if the fire looks smaller
The incoming officer needs the whole picture.
next: Lead a multi-company drill.
Write one after-action that names a next repetition.
Build evidence in My Career.

fire_officer_3.label: Fire Officer III
fire_officer_3.summary: Staff/chief-officer development: programs, planning, personnel systems, and multi-company operations. Confirm the exact FO III path with your certifying authority.
guide: Programs
Training, prevention, EMS, or special operations programs need goals, resources, and evaluation.
Planning
Budgets, staffing, and deployment are political and operational. Bring facts, options, and risks.
Personnel systems
Hiring, development, discipline, and wellness are systems—not one-off conversations.
Multi-company / multi-agency
ICS fluency, liaison, and clear objectives across organizations.
Evidence
Keep projects, after-actions, and outcomes. FO III is often demonstrated, not only tested.
cards: Organizational programs and planning, not only first-arriving tactics.
Problem, options, cost/risk, and a recommended path.
So a program can be improved or defended with more than anecdotes.
Policy, documentation, fairness, and legal/HR partnership.
Executive and officer courses that complement local certification—not replace it.
Translate operational needs into language elected officials and the public can use.
quiz: A training program with no evaluation is:
Programs need a way to see results.
When presenting a staffing option you should:
Show options, risks, and a recommendation
Happen only in the parking lot
Systems protect people and the organization.
Projects, ICS practice, and documented outcomes
The role is broader than a written exam.
next: Map your state FO III requirements.
Start one measurable program improvement.
Look at current NFA officer courses.

fire_officer_4.label: Fire Officer IV
fire_officer_4.summary: Executive-level fire-service leadership: policy, interagency relationships, and long-range organizational direction. Verify the local FO IV route.
guide: Policy
Executive officers shape policy that crews will live with. Clarity and legality matter.
Relationships
Elected officials, labor, neighboring agencies, and the public are part of the job.
Long-range view
Facilities, apparatus, staffing, and risk reduction play out over years.
Ethics
Conflicts of interest, transparency, and stewardship of public trust.
Still operational
Executive rank does not erase the need to understand fireground risk and ICS.
cards: Organizational direction and external relationships more than company tactics.
Clear, legal, trained, and enforceable—or it will fail in the field.
Large incidents and community risk reduction are rarely single-agency problems.
Develop people before vacancies force emergency promotions.
Useful supplements; they do not replace local certification rules.
Accurate, timely, and appropriate—without compromising investigations or personnel matters.
quiz: Policy has to work in practice.
Executive fire officers still need ICS fluency because:
Large incidents and multi-agency work require it
Rank does not remove operational literacy.
Community risk reduction at this level is:
A coordinated program with partners and measures
A slogan for the annual report
Develop people against the competencies of the next job
next: Confirm FO IV with your certifying agency.
Build a leadership portfolio in My Career.
Review NFA executive offerings.

fire_instructor_1.label: Fire Instructor I
fire_instructor_1.summary: Teach for job transfer: observable objectives, demonstration, coached repetitions, evaluation, and training-ground safety.
guide: Objectives
Describe observable learner behavior, conditions, and a standard—not 'understand fire behavior.'
Skill teaching
Explain, demonstrate, guide practice, allow repetitions, give specific feedback, and re-test.
Scenarios
Let learners discover information by acting. Debrief reasoning, not only the final answer.
Evaluation
Separate safety-critical failures from coaching points. Use a simple rubric.
Safety
Brief hazards, PPE, emergency signals, medical plan, and stop criteria before the evolution.
cards: An observable learner action rather than a vague word like understand.
Specific observation, the standard/impact, and another corrected repetition.

Information appears after the learner takes an appropriate action to discover it.
Attendance, objectives, performance, remediation, and lessons learned.

Decision training is stronger when learners gather information.

Stop criteria exist for a reason.

Instructor I teaching is successful when learners can:
Perform the skill or decision under the stated conditions

fire_instructor_2.label: Fire Instructor II
fire_instructor_2.summary: Program-level instruction: lesson design across a course, instructor coaching, evaluation systems, and training records that would survive review.
guide: Course design
Sequence lessons so skills and decisions build. Do not stack unrelated lectures.
Coach instructors
Instructor II often improves other instructors, not only recruits.
Evaluation systems
Consistent criteria, remediation paths, and integrity of testing.
Records
Objectives, attendance, performance, injuries, and after-action notes.
Live-fire / high-risk training
Follow current live-fire and high-risk training standards used by your agency. This deck is not a live-fire qualification.
cards: II leans into programs, other instructors, and evaluation systems.
How each lesson supports a job performance outcome.
A planned path back to the standard—not humiliation.
Same conditions, no teaching the test, and documented accommodations per policy.
Qualified instructors, safety officers, and current standards—not enthusiasm alone.

Coaching another instructor should focus on:

Your agency, AHJ, and current applicable standards
Do not treat this as live-fire cert.
Builds skills and decisions in a job-relevant order
Saves all practice for the last hour

Sit in on another instructor and give specific feedback.
Review your training records SOP.

fire_inspector_1.label: Fire Inspector I
fire_inspector_1.summary: Organized occupancy inspections using the code family your AHJ actually adopted. Cite current editions, not memory.
guide: Inspection sequence
Identify occupancy, construction, hazards, protection systems, and egress in a repeatable order.
Documentation
Write violations so a reasonable person could find the problem and the required correction.
Codes
Adopted edition and local amendments control. Confirm before citing.
Safety
Inspector PPE, dogs, industrial processes, and vacant buildings are real hazards.
Customer communication
Explain the life-safety why, not only the code number.
cards: A consistent walk-through order so you miss less.
Location, condition, code reference, and required action.
Citing the wrong year or amendment undermines the inspection.
Egress, extinguishers, blocked protection systems, and storage that changes occupancy hazard.
Requirements change with use and occupant load.
Comes from the AHJ, not from a FireOpsSim checklist.

Cite the newest book you own
Verify with the AHJ before writing the notice

fire_inspector_2.label: Fire Inspector II
fire_inspector_2.summary: Complex occupancies, plans coordination, and higher-quality documentation. Still AHJ- and edition-specific.
guide: Complex occupancies
Assembly, high-rise, industrial, and mixed use need more than a simple punch list.
Systems
Understand how detection, suppression, smoke control, and egress work together.
Plans and permits
Field conditions must match approved plans or be formally addressed.
Coordination
Building, fire, and life-safety reviewers often share an occupancy.
Quality
Photos, measurements, and clear notices reduce arguments later.
cards: II leans into complex occupancies and coordination, not only routine walk-throughs.
They locate the condition and support the written notice.
Egress and use requirements depend on it.
Built conditions that differ from approved plans need a process, not a shrug.

Firm on life safety, clear on corrections, no personal attacks.

Egress capacity, arrangement, and occupant load

Location, evidence, code basis, and correction
The owner has to be able to act.

fire_investigator.label: Fire Investigator
fire_investigator.summary: Scene safety, legal authority, systematic exam, and documentation before conclusions. Follow agency and prosecutor protocol.
guide: Authority first
Do not exceed legal authority or your assignment. Origin-and-cause work is not a hobby.
Safety
Structural compromise, utilities, crime, and contaminants can all be present.
Systematic exam
Document from the outside in. Observations before opinions.
Evidence
Preserve, photograph, and maintain chain of custody per agency protocol.
Interviews
Non-leading questions, accurate notes, and legal limits of your role.
cards: Scene safety, authority, and a systematic exam.
Overall, mid-range, and close-up with context/scale.
Who had the item, when, and why—per agency rules.
Structured and non-leading, within your legal role.
Professional development; they do not automatically grant legal authority.

Working a planned order and recording observations first

Practice a photo sequence on a training prop.
Do not invent chain-of-custody rules.

emt.label: EMT
emt.summary: BLS assessment, communication, documentation, and safety. Certification and state licensure are separate—confirm both.
guide: Scene and BSI
Scene safety and standard precautions before the patient exam.
Primary assessment
Find immediate life threats. Airway, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure as trained.
Trends
One vital is a snapshot. Change over time may show deterioration or response.
Handoff
Problem, relevant history, key findings, treatments, response, and concerns.
Scope
NREMT does not by itself authorize practice everywhere. State and local authorization control.

aemt.label: Advanced EMT
aemt.summary: AEMT scope is state-specific. Assessment still comes first. Confirm current scope, medical direction, and protocols.
guide: Scope first
AEMT interventions vary widely by state. Do not copy another system's skill list.
Assessment first
Advanced tools do not replace a primary assessment and trending.
Medication safety
Indication, contraindications, concentration, route, effect, and adverse response.
Airway support
Within authorized skills: positioning, ventilation, and adjuncts as trained and allowed.
ALS intercept
Know when to request paramedic/critical care resources early.

Performing a skill because you saw it once, not because protocol allows it.
Problem, what you did, response, remaining threats, and trends.
Follow current protocols and on-line/off-line direction as required.

paramedic.label: Paramedic
paramedic.summary: Disciplined ALS judgment: assessment first, medication/airway safety, ECG in context, leadership, and reassessment.
guide: Assessment first
Do not let the monitor replace a focused clinical assessment.
Airway
Positioning, ventilation, BVM, adjuncts, capnography concepts, and reassessment as trained.
Medication safety
Indication, contraindications, dose/concentration, route, effect, and adverse response.
ECG context
Integrate rhythm/12-lead findings with symptoms, exam, vitals, and serial change.
Leadership
Assign roles, communicate priorities, invite concerns, and revise the plan.

A clear problem, assessment, indication, risk/benefit, and complication plan.
Assessment, ventilation, hemorrhage control, movement, and communication remain foundational.

Treating a machine label without the patient context.
Clear priorities, role assignment, closed-loop communication, willingness to revise.

Reassess tracing and patient in context

bls.label: BLS / CPR
bls.summary: Issuer-dependent credential (AHA, Red Cross, or another provider your agency accepts). Use the current provider manual—not a generic algorithm dump.

Your department names the accepted card. Study that provider's current materials.
High-quality CPR
Rate, depth, recoil, and minimizing interruptions as taught in your course.
AED
Early defibrillation when indicated. Follow the prompts and your training.
Team CPR
Switch compressors, communicate, and keep the airway/ventilation plan coordinated.
After the card
Skills decay. Refresh before the card expires if your agency requires it sooner.

Use the old flowchart at work
